      <h2 class="workv-walk-title">What the evidence says</h2>
      <p class="workv-walk-sub">Three visual signals from the analysis, each connected to a practical question for People leaders. These are associations in an observational 2011 survey, not causal claims.</p>

          </div>
          <p class="workv-stepnote">Training was the only positive benefit lever in the final weighted model.</p>
        </article>

          <p class="workv-insighttext">Pay satisfaction had about 3.6 times the effect estimate of grouped pay band in the adjusted model.</p>
          <div class="workv-inset"><strong>Question for leaders</strong><br>Are employees satisfied with their pay experience, not only the amount they receive?</div>
        </article>
        <article class="workv-step">
          <div class="workv-stephead"><span class="workv-stepnum">03</span><div><strong>A smaller segment merits attention</strong><small>Weighted decision-tree sensitivity check</small></div></div>

          <div class="workv-act"><span class="workv-acticon">3</span><div><strong>Validate locally</strong><span>Test whether these historical signals hold in the organisation’s current data.</span></div></div>
        </div>

      <div class="workv-caveat"><span><strong>Evidence quality:</strong> 22/22 independent SQL checks passed; maximum R to SQL difference 0.005. WERS 2011 is observational, so association does not establish causation. The identified segment is a group-level signal, not an individual diagnosis. Flexitime missingness was 10.9% and job-sharing missingness was 17.5%, so those measures need particular caution.</span><strong>3.65 / 5 · 21,784 valid records</strong></div>
